There are many challenges that come with the job. Instead of explaining all of them I will boil it down to the major 2. For 1 the contracts you sign unless you are a trainee you should not be expect it to be fair or followed by normal laws. For example alot of staff were put on as part-time with promised consistent hours of around 30 or other agreed hours. That is not true in the slightest, it is more likely you will working more like a casual employee with changing hours each week. 1 week you might be working 26hrs but the next you'll get 10hrs. Problem 2. You are most likely not going to be trained well by staff as in most cases you will be understaffed or be trained for one shift then expected to work alone more then on. This is due to staff leaving/ understaffing/ management being unqualified or overwhelmed. I would recommend if you do decide to work for Subway that you ask to be put on a few shifts with other staff before you accept a shift by yourself. It will help in the long run with experience. These are the challenges and problems I witnessed through my experience at Subway and I truly hope someone reading this gets this knowledge and may help them in their own personal journey.

As a member of the field workforce in various roles over 35 years service, the greatest challenges revolved around giving service to the country in an industry that, by and large, was vital to the economic and social development of the community as a whole. As an individual working in a rapidly evolving technological field, the challenges related to maintaining currency with the latest technologies and systems were constant and unrelenting. These difficulties were met with resolve and persistence in order to gain the required mastery and proficiency necessary to continue working in the field. In addition to our daily activities, each of us in the field were obligated to maintain 24 hour availability when not on duty. The added stress of being required to respond to reports where there was a risk to public safety meant that we were never able to get sufficient rest in order to meet the next days challenges. The greatest challenges originated from within those parts of the organisation not directly associated with the customer-facing sections of the organisation. In addition to the inertia and restrictions placed on the field workforce by the management and administrative parts of the organisation, vested, sectional, and political interests affected the overall perceptions of how each individual in the field was regarded and treated by the community. These perceptions tended largely to be extremely negative, and coloured the opinions and reactions of the vast majority of the population. In that period between 1990 and 2007, I was working in a part of the organisation that was highly visible and therefore extremely vulnerable to the negative and anti-social attitudes and behaviours that were exhibited by a large proportion of the general populace throughout that period of time. Virtually all of the publicity generated from outside of the organisation was negative, derogatory and disparaging of the organisation, and each incident further inflamed the situations I found myself in each and every day. The organisations' management were disinclined to offer any explanation to counter any and all claims from any source against us , and this situation imbued most of us in the field with the belief that the work we were doing was not worthwhile or appreciated by any one person in the community.

There are many challenges that come with the job. Instead of explaining all of them I will boil it down to the major 2. For 1 the contracts you sign unless you are a trainee you should not be expect it to be fair or followed by normal laws. For example alot of staff were put on as part-time with promised consistent hours of around 30 or other agreed hours. That is not true in the slightest, it is more likely you will working more like a casual employee with changing hours each week. 1 week you might be working 26hrs but the next you'll get 10hrs. Problem 2. You are most likely not going to be trained well by staff as in most cases you will be understaffed or be trained for one shift then expected to work alone more then on. This is due to staff leaving/ understaffing/ management being unqualified or overwhelmed. I would recommend if you do decide to work for Subway that you ask to be put on a few shifts with other staff before you accept a shift by yourself. It will help in the long run with experience. These are the challenges and problems I witnessed through my experience at Subway and I truly hope someone reading this gets this knowledge and may help them in their own personal journey.

When I started at McDonald's, it was a great place to work. You could work with friends, the hours were flexible, and people were afforded the same opportunities for development. Recently, it's become more difficult to work within McDonald's, mainly due to their decisions to run more promotions, and to create unrealistic goals for the crew. It's becoming far too difficult for McDonald's employees to do their jobs, with constant introduction of new promotional items and products, and with this new kind of focus in some smaller stores to reduce the cost of labour. The stores have become frequently understaffed, the crew are expected to work even harder in a bid to keep up with the new gourmet range (with the same mimimum wage pay). In previous years, it was easy to progress within your own store; now, not so much. The process of progression can take months within individual stores, with management overlooking those loyal, hard working senior crew, to prioritise the younger crew who receive more shifts throughout the week. For McDonald's to be great once again, they really need to think about how their crew are being treated, and what they can do to keep crew motivated. Customet service is not easy.

Review Text: Most of the time, while working as a customer service supervisor, we were understaffed. Team members from other departments were supposed to help out during busy periods, but rarely did, which left customers complaining about ques and service quality as there was a rush to get customers out of the store. Service staff got tired of being stuck on register and often complained or regularly called in sick and cancelled shifts at the last minute, making these shifts very difficult to replace. A number of jobs were required of service staff in addition to customer service (for example cleaning, putting stock away, filling drink fridges and confectionery stands) and due to lack of staff these jobs were often left not done. Store managers and other higher up staff would then complain to me and my direct customer service manager, without recognizing that the reason tasks were not completed was due to lack of staff, not incompetence. Customers, particularly cigarette customers and refund customers tended to be difficult. Cigarette customers were often rude and demanding, as were refund customers. Some refund customers claimed to know our refund policy more than myself, who had been working there for over 7 years, and demanded free products, when this was not allowed.

If you’re a store manager at Aldi, forget about work-life balance. You’ll be the last one to get it. All those work-life balance rules? They’re mostly just for show. Burnout is right around the corner, especially with crazy goals and not enough staff. You’ll find yourself doing the work of four people. Directors and area managers have no clue what it’s really like in the stores. Honestly, they should try being a store manager for three months—I bet they wouldn’t last a month, even as a store assistant. And those yearly store manager conferences? Just a horror show. It’s like a competition to see who can be the most self-absorbed. Everyone acts like they’re on a talk show, but it really feels more like an episode of "The Office," with everyone channeling their inner Michael Scott. It’s just a bunch of kids in suits pretending to be important. They could easily turn those conferences into an email, and the money spent on them could be better used to support the stores or reward the staff—anything but boosting their own egos. Hearing “without you, we are nothing” feels empty when they’re at home dreaming up more ways to pile on the pressure for those of us who are working hard. They schedule important tasks like remerch on payroll days, which is just ridiculous. Choose easy days—Wednesdays and Thursdays—when there are no specials or payroll to worry about. The distribution center is already a mess, and things that should be simple turn into chaos. What’s really missing is a more human touch—actually caring about people. We’re not robots, but it seems like the company doesn’t really care about store workers. It’s all just a cover in the contract; they’re mainly focused on making money while those who genuinely care are struggling with their health. You’re replaceable, no matter how good you are, because the ones who really get ahead are usually the favorites. We all know how that goes, right? So if you value your health, this job might not be for you.

Few people know how to work stock efficiently, or properly merchandise stock, or stack a pallet with any sort of structural integrity, and the ones that do figured it out themselves. • Lack of safety standards: Blocked fire exits, hazardous stacking of boxes and stock on the shop floor and in the dock, some extremely heavy stock that you are expected to lift on your own, lack of mechanical aid for lifting/transporting heavy goods. The blatant disregard for any sort of workplace health and safety is honestly comical. • No loyalty to hardworking, long-term staff: This didn't apply to me as I wasn't there for all that long, but I saw a few people who had been there for years and were actually really good workers lose a bunch of hours because they didn't want to be contracted. Management values saving money far, far more than they value good workers. • Understaffed: This goes for pretty much every retail environment, but is especially true here. Lack of staff paired with all of the other things wrong with this workplace means that you are pretty much set up for failure every single day. I would rather be homeless and jobless than work for this nightmare of a company again.

This lack of engagement and accountability from those in managerial roles leads to a workplace culture that can only be described as cancerous.

One challenge I’ve noticed at ALPA is that remote staff can sometimes feel a real sense of isolation or disconnect from the wider community, especially in days when in-person energy is high. It’s genuinely difficult at times for remote team members to feel the same level of belonging and real-time camaraderie as those on-site. While we do a lot to bridge that gap and offer support—and I know we’re always here to help—it’s something that still needs attention. That said, recognizing this is what pushes us to keep finding new ways to include everyone, strengthen connections, and make sure every voice feels truly heard and valued, wherever they’re working from.

ALPA operates in a fast-paced, challenging environment. Those working remote need to work with challenges of limited resources, a different cultural context, surviving away from family, and problem-solving unexpected situations.

The complexity of operating across such a wide range of sectors and regions—from remote Northern Territory communities to Far North Queensland—can sometimes make it difficult to maintain consistent service delivery, cultural sensitivity, and community engagement. Balancing commercial success with social responsibility is no small feat, and there’s always a risk that some communities might feel underserved or disconnected if communication and feedback loops aren’t strong. That said, this isn’t a criticism of ALPA’s intentions—it’s more a reflection of the natural challenges that come with scaling up while staying true to grassroots values.

Working as IT support at the Arnhem Land Progress Aboriginal Corporation presents unique challenges, shaped by its remote locations and community-focused mission. One major difficulty is maintaining reliable internet and network infrastructure across isolated areas, where outages and limited connectivity can disrupt services. Delivering and setting up hardware in these regions also takes extra time and planning. Supporting a diverse workforce, many of whom may have limited experience with technology, requires clear and patient communication, as well as culturally sensitive training. You often need to troubleshoot a wide range of issues, from printers and laptops to network systems, sometimes without immediate access to advanced tools or backup. Balancing these technical demands with ALPA’s commitment to empowering Indigenous communities means your role isn’t just about fixing problems, it’s about enabling people, services, and businesses to thrive.

As the organisation grew at a rapid pace, the culture began to shift. The priority seemed to move away from quality practices and staff wellbeing and toward filling places as quickly as possible. New centres were opening back-to-back, and leadership roles were often given to people who didn’t have enough experience or training to handle them. Some centres were left operating with minimal input or direction from upper management. Expectations kept increasing, yet the support required to meet those expectations never followed.
